lesson.menu_title: The Way We Used to Work
lesson.menu_desc: How the last few years changed the job you do -- and the habits that went with them -- 32 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Way We Used to Work
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 6 -- The Way We Used to Work
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits
phases: The Way It Used to Be

listenings.text: Habits at work have a strange quality. While they last, they look like the only possible arrangement, and the moment they end nobody can quite explain why they were there. Think of the fax machine, or the eight-thirty meeting that existed so that everybody could report what they had written in an email the night before. People used to defend those things sincerely. They were not stupid and they were not lazy. The habit simply carried something real at the beginning, and then the reason quietly went away while the habit stayed. That is the useful question to ask about anything you still do every week. Not is this good, which is hard to answer, but this one: if it disappeared tomorrow, what exactly would we lose. If nobody in the room can say, you have found one.

Here is a small thing I dropped and never went back to. I used to print everything before a meeting. Every document, every set of numbers, one copy for each person, and I would do it the night before so that nothing went wrong in the morning. I told myself it was about being prepared, and part of it was. But the honest reason is that holding paper made me feel ready in a way that a screen did not, and that had nothing to do with the meeting at all. When it became impossible to do it, for about six months, I discovered that nobody had ever read them. Not once. What I actually needed was ten minutes of reading beforehand, and I had been buying that feeling with an hour of printing.

paras: Before 2020 the working week in most British offices had a shape that nobody questioned. You came in five days, you sat in roughly the same seat, and the building was about as full on a Monday as it was on a Thursday. People used to complain about the commute in the way you complain about the weather, and almost nobody expected any of it to change.

Then it changed overnight, for reasons that had nothing at all to do with how anybody felt about offices. Everybody worked from home, and a long list of things that were supposed to be impossible turned out to be merely unfamiliar.

What settled afterwards is more interesting than either extreme. The offices did not empty for good, and they did not fill up again either. A pattern appeared instead, and it is the same pattern in city after city: the middle of the week is busy and the edges are quiet. Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday are the days people come in. Monday and Friday are the days they do not. No company invented that rule and nobody wrote it down. It arrived on its own.

It is worth being precise about what actually disappeared, because it was not the office and it was not the meeting. What went is the assumption that being in the room is the same thing as working. That is a far bigger change than a day of the week, and if you look back on it in twenty years it is probably the part that will seem strange.
reading.source: Written for this lesson from public reporting on hybrid working patterns since 2020.
